props.subtitle: Get newcomers to their first real win fast — with the right onboarding method for the right audience
props.title: Onboarding Craft for IT Systems, Web Apps & Developer Experience

bullets: Access First: credentials, licenses, and environments are ready on day zero — waiting for access is the number-one onboarding killer
Time-to-First-Value: the only week-one metric that matters is how fast a newcomer completes one real, meaningful task
One Golden Path: a single canonical end-to-end journey beats a feature tour of every button
Progressive Disclosure: teach the next step only when the newcomer needs it — information firehoses create quit-points
Human Anchor: every method, even fully self-serve ones, needs a named human or office hours to land questions on
Measure the Friction: day-1 login success, golden-path completion, and ticket storms tell you where onboarding breaks
what.definition: Onboarding is the engineered path from 'a stranger is granted a account, a seat, or an API key' to 'this person has delivered something real without asking for help'. For an IT system that means staff and operators; for a Web App it means end users; for Developer Experience it means integrators building on your platform.
what.summary: Most onboarding fails the same way: a firehose of documentation, a pile of passwords, and a week of 'ping me if you're stuck'. This realm teaches the opposite discipline — grant access before day one, drive every newcomer to one golden-path task that produces real value in the first week, reveal complexity progressively, and measure the friction instead of guessing. Then pick the method that fits the audience: docs-first handbooks, buddy apprenticeship, cohort academies, self-serve in-app tours, or sandbox quests.

why.impact: Teams that pre-provision access and script a golden-path first task cut time-to-first-value from weeks to hours, slash newcomer support tickets, and dramatically improve both user activation and developer retention. Every onboarding method trades cost, consistency, and speed differently — choosing deliberately instead of defaulting to 'read the wiki' is the whole game.
why.summary: Bad onboarding is invisible until it shows up as a support queue full of 'how do I…' tickets, developers who quietly abandon your API after an afternoon of setup, and new staff who spend a month afraid to touch production. Onboarding is the highest-leverage moment in the whole lifecycle: attention is high, habits are unformed, and everything you teach sticks.

categories.analogy: A hotel check-in: nobody tours you through the HVAC plant — you get your key, your room is warm, and you're asleep in twenty minutes.
categories.description: People who must complete business tasks in your Web App. For them, good onboarding means reaching their first successful task without ever leaving the product or opening a ticket.
categories.details: End users do not care how the system works; they care whether they can finish their job today. Onboarding for them is product work: a guided first-run flow, sensible sample data, one golden-path task (create the first project, invite the first teammate, run the first report), and help that appears exactly when they hover over the confusing button. Every extra login, jargon word, or blank screen is a quit-point where users quietly churn. Pros and cons of each delivery method (tours, docs, cohorts) are weighed later in Track 2 — the doctrine is the same: first value inside the product, fast.
inScope: Guided first-run experience and activation moments
Sample data so the app is never a terrifying blank page
Contextual help at the exact point of confusion
outOfScope: Server architecture the user will never see
Admin configuration and user-management screens
categories.primaryFocus: First successful business task inside the product
categories.subtitle: Customers & business users
categories.title: Web App End Users

categories.analogy: Flight school: ground school, then dual controls, then a solo — never 'here's the keys, good luck'.
categories.description: People hired to run, support, and operate the IT system from the inside. For them, onboarding is a supervised climb from 'afraid to touch production' to 'on-call and trusted'.
categories.details: Staff and operators onboard into a socio-technical system: tools, credentials, runbooks, escalation chains, and unwritten traditions. The failure mode is the month-long silent soak — a new hire reads the wiki, watches senior people, and touches nothing real for weeks. Good internal onboarding pre-provisions every account on day zero, pairs the newcomer with a buddy for the first incidents, and graduates them through deliberately graded real tasks: first a low-risk change with a witness, then a supervised deploy, then the pager. Their manual is the runbook; their exam is a real shift.
inScope: Day-zero accounts, licenses, VPN, and toolchain readiness
Runbooks, escalation paths, and incident rituals
Buddy shadowing and graduated production privileges
outOfScope: Marketing messaging about the product
Billing plan comparisons the employee never touches
categories.primaryFocus: Graded real tasks from supervised change to independent on-call
categories.subtitle: Employees of the IT system
categories.title: Internal Staff & Operators

categories.analogy: A test drive with the keys in hand: if the engine doesn't start in the first turn, the buyer walks to the dealership next door.
categories.description: People building on top of your platform or API. For them the onboarding IS the product trial: setup, auth, and the first successful call decide whether they stay or quietly leave.
categories.details: Developers onboard themselves or they don't onboard at all. Every minute of setup friction, every broken quickstart snippet, every 'contact sales to get an API key' is a funnel stage where integrators abandon you — and they will not file a ticket, they will just leave. Good DX onboarding means: keys minted in self-serve minutes, a quickstart that works on a clean machine in under fifteen, a sandbox with realistic test data, generated API references, and a visible path from hello-world to production. Time-to-first-call is the developer's time-to-first-value.
inScope: Self-serve signup, keys, and a real sandbox with test data
Quickstart that is CI-tested to work on a clean machine
Generated API references, error catalogs, and changelogs
outOfScope: Sales-gated trials that add days to the first call
Slide decks about architecture instead of runnable code

items.text: Principle 2 — First Value in Week One: drive to one real win fast

children.text: Design ONE scripted end-to-end route through the system that every newcomer walks
A tour of every button produces fatigue; one deep task produces competence

items.text: Principle 3 — One Golden Path: a single canonical journey beats a feature tour

children.text: Teach the next step at the moment the newcomer reaches it, never three screens ahead
Information firehoses create quit-points; a short path with deeper links respects the newcomer's attention

items.text: Principle 4 — Progressive Disclosure: reveal complexity only when it is needed

children.text: Even fully self-serve onboarding needs office hours, a buddy, or a channel where questions land on a real person
Unanswered questions at hour three are where motivation dies — not at hour zero

items.text: Principle 5 — Human Anchor: every path ends at a named human

children.text: Track day-1 login success, golden-path completion rate, and where help tickets storm
Fix the biggest measured quit-point before adding any new onboarding content

items.text: Principle 6 — Measure the Friction: instrument the path, watch where they stall

challenges.prompt: Assemble the six onboarding principles in their correct order of operation:

categories.analogy: A well-written restaurant menu: necessary, referenceable, cheap to reprint — but nobody learns to cook from the menu alone.
categories.description: The classic: a written, searchable path — quickstart, handbook, runbooks — that newcomers read and follow at their own pace.
categories.details: PROS: cheapest per learner and infinitely reusable; searchable and versionable; survives every hire and reorg; scales to any headcount without scheduling. CONS: passive — nothing forces engagement, and 'did you read the wiki?' is the epitaph of a thousand failed onboardings; rots within a sprint if not owned in CI; tells you how to fish but not which lake; zero human connection, so confused readers quit silently. Verdict: the backbone every other method links back to, but never the only method.
inScope: PRO — near-zero marginal cost per new learner, scales to thousands
PRO — searchable, versioned, and reviewable like code (docs-as-code)
PRO — the durable reference every other method points to
outOfScope: CON — passive: no engagement guarantee, quiet quit-points
CON — rots fast without a CI-owned maintainer
CON — no human anchor for the questions between the lines
categories.subtitle: Wikis, handbooks & runbooks
categories.title: Docs-First Handbook

categories.analogy: Flight school dual controls: the fastest way to competence, but every hour consumes a certified instructor.
categories.description: A named senior person adopts the newcomer: shadowing first, then the buddy watches the newcomer drive real tasks.
categories.details: PROS: carries the tacit knowledge no handbook holds (which dashboards matter, who to ping, what 'usually fine' means); instant feedback loop; strongest retention and trust of any method; naturally enforces the Human Anchor principle. CONS: does not scale — each buddy carries one or two newcomers at a time and pays real focus tax on their own work; quality varies entirely with the buddy's people skills; informal versions burn out the friendliest senior engineer. Verdict: the gold standard for internal staff and operators; use it deliberately and cap the load per buddy.
inScope: PRO — transmits tribal knowledge, judgment, and escalation culture
PRO — highest engagement, retention, and psychological safety
PRO — real-time correction of bad habits before they set
outOfScope: CON — does not scale; heavy focus tax on senior staff
CON — quality is as good as the busiest volunteer
CON — informal buddy systems quietly burn out helpers
categories.subtitle: One-on-one shadowing & pairing
categories.title: Buddy Apprenticeship

categories.analogy: Trade school: brilliant cohort energy and a certified baseline, but the semester starts in September whether you like it or not.
categories.description: Scheduled batches — a week-one bootcamp, a weekly class, an internal academy — where a group learns the system together with an instructor and shared exercises.
categories.details: PROS: guarantees a consistent, complete baseline for every newcomer; scheduled time is protected time, so engagement is high; creates a peer cohort — the loneliest onboarding failure cured instantly; instructor accumulates and improves the material. CONS: expensive per head (instructor hours, rooms, prep); calendar-locked — a solo hire waits weeks for the next batch or drowls alone; pace is set by the slowest attendee; content goes stale unless someone owns revisions. Verdict: ideal for campus hires and platform rollouts to many teams at once; terrible for the one senior developer joining Tuesday.
inScope: PRO — guaranteed consistent curriculum for every newcomer
PRO — peer cohort cures isolation and seeds future help networks
PRO — protected calendar time drives real engagement
outOfScope: CON — high per-head cost and instructor burden
CON — calendar-locked: bad fit for lone or urgent hires
CON — one pace fits all; fast learners idle, slow learners drown
categories.primaryFocus: Consistent baseline via scheduled group instruction
categories.subtitle: Batch training & bootcamps
categories.title: Cohort Academy

categories.analogy: Video-game tutorial levels: learn the controls by playing the first room, not by reading the box.
categories.description: Onboarding built into the product itself: first-run checklists, overlay tours, and empty-state coaching that teach while the newcomer does the real task.
categories.details: PROS: teaches inside the artifact at the moment of need — the purest form of progressive disclosure; zero marginal cost per learner and instant updates for every user at once; measurable to the click (completion, drop-off, time-to-activation); the only method that scales to millions of end users. CONS: engineering and design cost up front; fragile against UI churn (stale tours mispoint at buttons); covering every feature in tours breeds banner blindness and 'skip all'; cannot carry judgment, edge cases, or why. Verdict: the default for Web App end users and self-serve DX; pair it with docs for depth and a human anchor for doubt.
inScope: PRO — scales to any user count with near-zero marginal cost
PRO — teach at the exact moment of need; fully instrumentable
PRO — shipping a fix to the tour reaches every user instantly
outOfScope: CON — upfront engineering cost and UI-churn fragility
CON — tour fatigue: users learn to click 'skip all'
CON — cannot teach judgment, policy, or the edge cases
categories.primaryFocus: Learning by doing inside the live product
categories.subtitle: First-run checklists & overlay tours
categories.title: Self-Serve In-App Tours

categories.analogy: A driving course with traffic cones and an inflatable wall: all the reflexes of the real road, none of the funerals.
categories.description: A safe, seeded practice environment where onboarding is a game: a quest board of graded challenges, hidden Easter eggs, and a final 'boss' task that proves competence.
categories.details: PROS: learning by doing with zero blast radius — newcomers break the sandbox happily and remember why; intrinsically motivating and genuinely fun, the anti-dread onboarding; exposes the curious, who explore past the minimum path and become future experts. CONS: the most expensive method to build and the most expensive to keep fresh (seeded data rots, environments drift, quests go stale); grading and cheating need design; can trivialize if the quests are shallow or feel like chores with pixel art. Verdict: spectacular as the spine of a cohort academy or a DX platform trial; wasteful as the only door for a user who just needs to do their job today.
inScope: PRO — safe-to-break practice with memorable, hands-on learning
PRO — high motivation; surfaces the curious future experts
PRO — graded quests make competence objective, not vibes
outOfScope: CON — highest build cost and constant environment-freshness tax
CON — shallow quests become pixel-art chores fast
CON — overkill when the learner just needs today's task done

audience.prompt: Who is being onboarded right now?

leaf.explanation: Apprenticeship carries the escalation culture no handbook holds, and graded real tasks convert reading into trusted competence. Cap each buddy at two newcomers to dodge the burnout con.
leaf.recommendation: Buddy apprenticeship with graduated privileges: shadow incidents, then drive with a witness, then the supervised pager — with runbooks as the spine.
tradeoffs: Real focus tax on senior operators
Buddy quality varies; brief the buddies on what to teach

leaf.explanation: Apprenticeship's pros — tacit knowledge, trust, highest retention — justify its focus tax only when each account is worth the hours. The recording amortizes the cost into self-serve assets.
leaf.recommendation: Buddy-style live onboarding sessions for each account, recorded and clipped into the handbook, with a self-serve tour left behind for their teammates.
tradeoffs: Does not scale past a handful of accounts
Quality varies with the people skills of whoever runs the session

leaf.explanation: Developers self-onboard or leave quietly; time-to-first-successful-API-call is their first value. Docs-first is the backbone here, but every step must be runnable, not readable.
leaf.recommendation: Self-serve DX path: keys minted in minutes, a CI-tested quickstart to a first successful call in under fifteen, a seeded sandbox with test data, and generated API references.
tradeoffs: Quickstarts need CI tests or they rot within a sprint
Sandbox data seeding is an ongoing tax

leaf.explanation: Sandbox quests deliver zero-blast-radius practice and objective competence — the taught pros — and the boss-task review supplies the human anchor.
leaf.recommendation: Sandbox quests: a seeded practice environment with a graded quest board ending in a boss task reviewed by a senior.
tradeoffs: Building and re-seeding the playground is the costliest method to keep fresh
Shallow quests become pixel-art chores; design the boss task with care

leaf.explanation: The in-app tour method's taught pros — near-zero marginal cost, teach-at-the-moment-of-need, instant fixes shipped to everyone — fit a large, stable audience. Instrument completion and drop-off per the Measure-the-Friction principle.
leaf.recommendation: Self-serve in-app checklists and first-run tours driving one golden-path task, with sample data so the app is never a blank page.
tradeoffs: Upfront engineering cost for the tour layer
Needs a human anchor (office hours or a channel) for the questions tours cannot answer

leaf.explanation: Tour fragility against UI churn is the documented con: keep the overlay surface tiny and let searchable, CI-owned docs absorb the change velocity.
leaf.recommendation: Lightweight in-app checklists for the golden path only, plus a docs-as-code handbook carrying the depth, linked at the point of need.
tradeoffs: Docs need a CI-owning maintainer or they rot
Two artifacts to keep pointed at the same golden path

props.intro: It is 9:10 on Monday morning. Forty newcomers — end users, operators, and five platform developers — are logged in (most of them) to a Wi-Fi guest network, a wiki nobody has refreshed since last quarter, and a Slack channel called #newest-hires. As the onboarding lead, what do you do first?

outcome.lesson: The information firehose with no human anchor is the doctrine's textbook failure: passive content plus unanswered questions at hour three is exactly where motivation dies.
outcome.verdict: By lunch the handbook has 3 comments, the #newest-hires channel has 27 questions, and you have answered none of them. Two developers have already quietly left to 'explore the API later'.

outcome.lesson: Heroic manual provisioning is the anti-pattern the provisioning flow exists to automate: SSO group rules and self-serve key minting scale; your browser tabs do not.
outcome.verdict: You personally fix 14 people's access by 11pm. The remaining 26 wait for the hero to recover. Next Monday's cohort gets nothing, because you are asleep.

outcome.lesson: Waiting-for-access is the number-one onboarding killer: Access First means credentials exist before day one, and 'soon' is how first value slips from week one to never.
outcome.verdict: The queue is honest, at least. It is also three weeks deep. Week one becomes week three of 'ping me when you're stuck', and three newcomers quit-point to silence.

outcome.lesson: An architecture tour is not onboarding. Each audience needed its own first value — a task, a graded change, a first API call — not a shared context nobody asked for.
outcome.verdict: You covered the microservices diagram beautifully. The operators wanted their runbooks, the end users wanted their first task, and the developers wanted their API keys. All three got slides instead.

choices.text: Personality-provision all 40 people yourself, one browser tab at a time
Fix the fastest scripted wins first: mint dev keys via the self-serve flow, fill the sample workspace, file the privileged grants properly
File everything into the normal IT queue and tell people to expect access 'soon'

result-triage.prompt: Triage reveals the truth: the 5 developers have no API keys, 3 operators are missing production-reach entitlements, and the end users' sample workspace is empty. You have one day and one team. Where do you spend it?

outcome.lesson: This is the doctrine in one day: access unblocked through automation, one golden-path task per audience to first value, progressive depth via the handbook, and a scheduled human anchor for the questions. Measure who stalls next and fix that first.
outcome.verdict: By 3pm the developers ship their first test call against seeded sandbox data, the end users complete their first real record in a populated workspace, and the operators are shadowing an afternoon incident with runbooks open. You book office hours for Thursday and pin the handbook's single golden-path page in the channel.

choices.text: Send everyone the wiki link and a 40-page handbook to read while you put out fires
Stop everything and triage access: who can actually log in and touch a real environment today?
Book the afternoon for a full architecture presentation so everyone shares context

props.title: Monday Without a Path

terms.detailedDefinition: Measured from day zero (or key issuance for developers) to the first genuine win: a submitted record, a safe production change, a successful API call. Everything else in onboarding is a leading indicator of this number.

dialogue.aiQuestion: What was the median hours from day zero to each newcomer's first real task?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Coverage is not completion; nobody has shipped a real task yet.
dialogue.user: We covered every feature in the kickoff deck!

terms.shortDefinition: How fast a newcomer completes one real, meaningful task — the doctrine's only week-one metric.
terms.whyItMatters: It converts 'onboarding feels fine' into a number you can drive down; teams that instrument it stop writing handbook pages and start removing walls.

terms.detailedDefinition: One canonical route through the system — create, configure, run, export — maintained like production code, with deeper optional routes branching only after it succeeds.
terms.shortDefinition: The single scripted end-to-end journey every newcomer walks first, chosen to produce a real win.
terms.whyItMatters: A tour of every button produces fatigue; one deep golden path produces competence, and its completion rate is the sharpest leading indicator of friction.

terms.detailedDefinition: Joiner tickets drive SSO group rules and self-serve key minting so the newcomer's first action is work, not a provisioning queue. Production-reach roles get vault-approved grants in the same window.
terms.shortDefinition: Everything done before day one: accounts, licenses, environments, and entitlements provisioned and smoke-tested.
terms.whyItMatters: Waiting-for-access is the number-one onboarding killer; pre-boarding is Principle 1 made real.

terms.detailedDefinition: Different per audience: the end user's first real record, the operator's first supervised safe change, the developer's first successful call. It is defined before it is measured, never guessed afterward.
terms.shortDefinition: The deliberately designed 'aha' where the product's value becomes personal for a newcomer.
terms.whyItMatters: You cannot shorten time-to-first-value if you never wrote down what 'value' is; the activation moment is the finish line you instrument.

terms.detailedDefinition: The opposite of the information firehose: short paths with deeper links, tour steps at the point of confusion, advanced options hidden until the golden path succeeds.
terms.shortDefinition: Revealing the next level of complexity only at the moment the newcomer needs it.
terms.whyItMatters: Every unneeded fact shown early is a quit-point manufactured on purpose; attention is the onboarding budget.

terms.detailedDefinition: Questions are unanswered documentation: where the cohort asks in a burst is precisely where the golden path, tour, or entitlement broke.

dialogue.aiQuestion: What did the day-one smoke test just start failing for everyone?
dialogue.aiThoughts: That is not noise, that is a map.
dialogue.user: Why is #newest-hires suddenly asking about SSO seventeen times an hour?

terms.shortDefinition: A spike of help-channel and support questions from the current newcomer cohort, tagged and trended as a friction signal.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the cheapest quit-point detector you have — the newcomers are telling you out loud where they stalled.

terms.detailedDefinition: The gamified onboarding method: newcomers break the playground happily, climb a quest board of real tasks, and prove competence on the boss task with zero blast radius.
terms.shortDefinition: A graded challenge in a safe, seeded practice environment, ending in a senior-reviewed 'boss task'.
terms.whyItMatters: It converts anxious observation into motivated doing for staff and operators — at the cost of keeping a playground forever fresh.

terms.detailedDefinition: Even fully self-serve methods route their last resort to a person: office hours, a buddy rota, or a staffed channel. A FAQ link is explicitly not an anchor.
terms.shortDefinition: The named human, buddy, or staffed office-hours channel every onboarding path must end at.
terms.whyItMatters: Unanswered questions at hour three are where motivation dies; the anchor is the doctrine's insurance policy against silent quit-points.

challenges.explanation: Correct! Principle 1 grants day-zero access, Principle 2 drives one golden-path task in week one, and Principle 4 reveals complexity through progressive disclosure — the handbook firehose is the anti-pattern.
challenges.template: The doctrine grants {zone-1} before day one, drives every newcomer to one {zone-2} task in week one, and reveals complexity through {zone-3}.

challenges.explanation: Correct! In-app tours carry the mass audience, apprenticeship carries the high-risk climb (watching for burnout), and the handbook is the spine everything links to — bootcamps are calendar-locked and cost-per-head.
challenges.template: At hundred-thousand-user scale only {zone-1} scale at near-zero marginal cost; high-risk operator roles climb best via {zone-2}; and the docs-first {zone-3} is the backbone, never the only door.

challenges.explanation: Correct! Time-to-first-value is the north star the whole stack feeds; ticket storms are the cohort telling you where the path broke; and the manual credential-fix loop earns its name from the day-one 4003 that exposes it. Pages-read counts are the vanity metric the realm rejects.
